(p-535)

Surah "Al-Ma'arij" (The Ascending Stairways)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿A questioner asked for a punishment to befall﴾. He was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who said: "If this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment." Or it was the Prophet (ﷺ) who called for the descent of punishment. Since "sa'ala" (asked) was made to carry the meaning of "da'a" (called for), it took its construction, as if it had been said: "A caller called for."

﴿a punishment that will surely befall﴾ — from your saying "da'a bi-kadha" (he called for such-and-such) when he requested it and sought it. And from this is His (Exalted) saying: ﴿calling therein for every kind of fruit﴾ [al-Dukhan: 55]. "Wa sa'ala" (sa'ala without a hamza) is read by the people of Madina and Syria, and it is also from "al-su'al" (asking), except that it was lightened by softening. And "sa'il" (questioner) with a hamza is agreed upon (by the reciters).

For the disbelievers (lil-kafirin), an attribute of "punishment" (ʿadhab): i.e., with a punishment that befalls and is destined for the disbelievers,

There is not for it (laysa lahu), for that punishment,

any repeller (dafiʿ), one who turns it back.

"From Allah" — connected either to "vā'iq" (meaning: befalling from Him) or to "dāfi'" (meaning: there is no repeller of it from His direction, may He be exalted, when its time comes),

"Lord of the ascents" — i.e., the ascending stairways of the heaven for the angels, plural of "ma'raj" (ma'raj being the place of ascent). (p-536) Then he described the ascents and the extent of their distance in height and elevation, saying:

﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾ (ascend), meaning "تَصْعَدُ" (rises), and with the letter ya' (read as "yaʿruju") it is the reading of ʿAlī.

﴿المَلائِكَةُ والرُوحُ﴾ (the angels and the Spirit): "the Spirit" means Jibril (peace be upon him). He is singled out for mention after the general term because of his excellence and nobility. Or it means a creation who are guardians over the angels, just as the angels are guardians over us. Or it means the spirits of the believers at the time of death.

﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ (to Him): to His Throne and the place from which His command descends.

﴿فِي يَوْمٍ﴾ (on a day): this is connected to "تَعْرُجُ" (ascend).

﴿كانَ مِقْدارُهُ خَمْسِينَ ألْفَ سَنَةٍ﴾ (whose measure is fifty thousand years): of the years of this world, if anyone other than an angel ascends in it. Or it is connected to "واقِعٍ" (occurring), meaning: it occurs on a long day whose measure is fifty thousand years of your years, and this is the Day of Resurrection. Either its length is an extension, due to its severity for the disbelievers, or it is literally so. It has been said: "On it there are fifty stations, each station a thousand years, and for the believers that is no more than the time between the Zuhr (midday prayer) and the ʿAṣr (afternoon prayer)."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 5:

﴿فاصْبِرْ﴾ ("So be patient"), related to "asked a questioner" (sa'ala sa'il), because the hastening of al-Nadr (al-Nadr ibn al-Harith) for the punishment was only in the manner of mockery of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and denial of the revelation, and that was among the things that distressed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he was commanded to be patient with it,

﴿صَبْرًا جَمِيلا﴾ ("with beautiful patience"), without impatience (jaza') and without complaint (shakwa).

Inna-hum (indeed they): i.e., the disbelievers,

yarawnahu (they see it): i.e., the punishment, or the Day of Resurrection,

ba'idan (as far off): i.e., impossible (mustahilan).
"And We see it as near," [it being] certain to occur without doubt. So what is meant by "far" is that which is far from possibility, and by "near" that which is near to it.

Naṣaba ﴿yawma takūnu al-samā'u﴾ (the phrase "the day the sky becomes") is governed by "qarīban" (soon), meaning: it is possible on that day [that it will happen]. Or it is a substitution (badal) for "fī yawmin" (on a day), according to those who make it dependent on "wāqi'" (will occur).

﴿Ka-l-muhl﴾: like the dregs (durdī) of olive oil, or like molten silver in its changing of colours.

﴿And the mountains will be like wool, carded and dyed⦆... 

Translation:

﴿And the mountains will be like wool﴾, i.e., like wool dyed in various colours, because the mountains are of varied streaks: white and red, their colours differing, and jet-black (ghara'ib sud). So when they are crumbled to dust and set flying through the air, they resemble fluffed-up wool (al-ihn al-manfush) when the wind scatters it.

(p-٥٣٧) ﴿And no close friend will ask a close friend﴾, meaning no relative will ask about a relative, because each is preoccupied with himself. And according to al-Bazzi and al-Burjumi, with a damma on the yā' (يُسْألُ, read as passive *yus'alu*), meaning: no relative will be asked about a relative, i.e., he will not be held responsible for him, and will not be taken to account for his sin.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 11:

﴿They will be made to see them﴾: it is a description (ṣifah), meaning: a close friend (ḥamīm) who will see them, making them known to one another; or it is a resumed clause (mustaʾnaf), as if, when He said, "and no close friend will ask a close friend," it was said: "Perhaps he will not see him," so it was said: "They will be made to see them, but, because of their preoccupation, they will not be able to ask one another." The wāw is the pronoun of the first close friend (ḥamīm), and "hum" is the pronoun of the second close friend, meaning: close friends will see close friends, so they will not be hidden from one another. The two pronouns are in the plural although they refer to the two close friends, because faʿīl (ḥamīm) takes the place of the plural.

﴿The guilty one wishes﴾: he wishes, i.e., the polytheist (al-mushrik) wishes. It is a resumed clause (mustaʾnaf), or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the raised pronoun or the object pronoun in "yubaṣṣarūnahum" (they will be made to see them).

﴿that he could ransom himself from the punishment of that Day by his children﴾: it is read with a fatḥah (bi-l-fatḥ, i.e., "yaftadī" with a fatḥah on the ḍād/ending is not indicated here) as Madanī reads it, and with construction for the idāfah (ʿalā al-binā' li-l-idāfah) to a non-declinable (ghayr mutamakkin) noun, [reading "yawma'idhin" with the vowel of construction].

﴿with his sons﴾

**Translation:**

﴿And his wife﴾, his spouse,

﴿and his brother﴾

﴿And his kinsfolk﴾, and his nearest clan (ʿashīrah), al-adnayn,

﴿who shelters him﴾: who gathers him (taḍummuhu) by belonging to it. And without hamza (the glottal stop), it is read "یزید" (يَزِيدُ, Yazīd).

﴿And whoever is on the earth, all of them,﴾ of the people,

﴿then [it would] deliver him,﴾ al-iftida' (ransoming), coordinated (ʿatf) with "يَفْتَدِي" (yaftadi, "he would ransom himself").

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 15:

﴿Kalla﴾ (By no means!), a deterrent to the criminal from wishing to be ransomed, and a warning that ransom will not benefit him, nor will it save him from the punishment.

﴿Innaha﴾ (Indeed, it), [the pronoun refers to] "inna al-nar" (indeed the Fire), and the mention of the punishment indicates it. Or it is an ambiguous pronoun (damir mubham) whose meaning is expressed by the predicate that follows it. Or it is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-qissa), [meaning "the matter" or "the story"].

﴿Laza﴾ (Blazing Flame), a proper name (ʿalam) for the Fire.

﴿Plucking out﴾, read by Hafs and al-Mufaddal, is in the accusative as a *hal mu'akkidah* (emphatic circumstantial accusative), or in the accusative of specification (*ikhtisas*), for the sake of intensifying the terror. The other readers read it in the nominative, as a second predicate (*khabar*) following the predicate of *inna* (the particle of emphasis), or as [the predicate of] "it is a plucker" (*hiya nazza'ah*).

﴿for the extremities﴾: the limbs of the human being, such as the hands and the feet. Or it is the plural of *shawah* (*shawah*), which is the skin of the head. It pulls it out with a pulling, so it separates it, then it returns to what it was.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 17:

﴿Tad'ū﴾ (it calls), by their names: "O unbeliever, O hypocrite, come to me, come to me"; or it destroys, from their saying "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning: God destroy you. Or, since its destination is toward it, it is made as though it called him.

﴿Man adbara﴾ (who turned his back), from the truth;

﴿Wa tawalla﴾ (and turned away), from obedience.
And he gathered [wealth], ﴿and hoarded it﴾ — he put it into a container, and did not pay God's due from it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 19–21:

﴿Indeed, mankind﴾: by it is meant the species (jins), so that the exception of those who pray (al-musallin) from it may be valid.

﴿was created anxious (halu'an)﴾. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both: "Its explanation is what follows it: ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed (jaza'an)﴾ ﴿and when good touches him, he is withholding (mana'an)﴾." And "al-hala'" (anxiety, impatience): quick distress upon contact with what is disliked, and quick withholding upon contact with good. Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir asked Tha'lab about al-hala', and he said: "Allah (Exalted is He) has explained it, and there can be no explanation clearer than His explanation." It is the one who, when evil reaches him, displays extreme distress, and when good reaches him, is stingy with it and withholds it from people. This is his natural disposition (tab'), and he is commanded to oppose his disposition and conform to His law (shar'). And "al-sharr" (evil) means harm and poverty, and "al-khayr" (good) means abundance and wealth, or illness and health.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 23:

﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾: over their prayers, the five daily prayers.

﴿Constant﴾: i.e., those who guard them diligently, at their appointed times. Related from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him).
"And those in whose wealth is a known right," meaning the zakat, because it is a determined and known amount; or a charity which a man assigns upon himself, paying it at known times.

For the beggar who asks, and the deprived.

Al-Nasafi's gloss: "For the beggar" refers to the one who asks. "And the deprived" refers to the one who abstains from asking, so he is thought to be wealthy and therefore is deprived (of charity).
And those who affirm the Day of Religion (yawm al-din) — that is, the Day of Recompense and Reckoning, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 27:

﴿And those who are, from the punishment of their Lord, apprehensive﴾ — fearful. He interjected with his statement:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 28:

﴿Indeed, the punishment of their Lord is not something to be felt secure from﴾, with the hamza (read with hamza), except according to Abu 'Amr, meaning: it is not fitting for anyone, however much he exerts himself in worship and obedience, to feel secure from it, and he should remain balanced between fear (khawf) and hope (raja').
(p-٥٣٩)﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 30:

﴿Except from their spouses,﴾ i.e., their wives,

﴿or what their right hands possess,﴾ i.e., their female slaves,

﴿for indeed they are not blameworthy,﴾ for leaving off guarding (their chastity).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 31:

﴿Whoever seeks beyond that﴾: he seeks a means of sexual gratification (mankah),

﴿beyond that﴾: i.e., other than wives and those whom the right hand possesses (al-mamlukat),

﴿those are the transgressors (al-'adun)﴾: those who exceed what is lawful (halal) to what is unlawful (haram). This verse indicates the prohibition of temporary marriage (mut'ah), intercourse with males, with animals, and masturbation by hand (al-istimna' bi-l-kaff).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 70, verse 32:

﴿And those who are faithful to their trusts﴾. "لِأمانَتِهِمْ" (*li-amanatihim*, in the singular), read by Makki. It covers the trusts of the Law (*al-sharʿ*, divine law), and the trusts between people.

﴿and their covenant﴾, meaning their covenants. This includes the covenants made with creatures, vows (*al-nudhur*), and oaths (*al-ayman*).

﴿who maintain﴾, meaning who guard, who are not treacherous and do not break them. It is also said: "al-amanat" are what the intellects indicate, and "al-ʿahd" is what the Messenger brought.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 33:

﴿And those who are in their testimonies﴾, "Hafs, Sahl and Ya'qub [read: bi-shahadatihim]",

﴿upright﴾: they establish them before the judges, without bias toward a relative or a person of high standing, and without favoring the strong over the weak, displaying firmness in religion and a desire to revive the rights of the Muslims.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 34:

﴿And those who are steadfast in their prayers.﴾ He repeated the mention of prayer (al-salah) to show that it is more important, or because the first refers to the obligatory prayers (al-fara'id) and the second to the voluntary prayers (al-nawafil). It has also been said: "al-dawam 'alayha" (constancy in it) means performing it often, and "al-muhafazah 'alayha" (guarding it) means not neglecting it beyond its appointed times. Or: "al-dawam 'alayha" means performing it at its proper times, and "al-muhafazah 'alayha" means preserving its pillars (arkan), its obligatory elements (wajibat), its sunnas, and its etiquettes (adab).

Those ﴿who are such﴾, the possessors of these attributes,

﴿are honored in gardens﴾. Both of these are predicates (khabar).

Fa-mā lahum (fa-māli), written separately (maftūlan, "detached"), in conformity with the codex of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him,

﴿who disbelieve, before you﴾, i.e., toward you (naḥwaka). The governed element (maʿmūl) is ﴿hastening﴾ (muhṭiʿīna), meaning hurrying (musriʿīna), and it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "those who disbelieved" (alladhīna kafarū).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 37:

﴿From the right and from the left﴾, i.e., from the right of the Prophet (ﷺ) and from his left.

﴿Groups﴾ (ʿizīn), a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: scattered factions. It is the plural of ʿizah, and its origin is ʿiznah, as if each faction claims kinship (taʿtazī) to other than that to which the other one claims kinship, so they are dispersed. The polytheists (al-mushrikūn) would gather around the Prophet (ﷺ) in circles upon circles and groups upon groups, listening and mocking his speech, and saying: "If these people enter Paradise as Muhammad says, then we will surely enter it before them." So the verse was revealed:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 38:

﴿Does every one of them aspire to be admitted﴾ — with the yā' vowelled with a ḍammah and the khā' with a fatḥah (yudkhala, in the passive), except for al-Mufaḍḍal's reading — ﴿into a garden of bliss﴾, like the believers.

"Nay," a rebuke to them for their greed to enter Paradise.

﴿Indeed, We created them from that which they know.﴾ That is, from a foul drop of semen. It is for this reason that He left it vague, to indicate that it is a matter one is shy to mention. So from where do they derive nobility, claim precedence, and say, "We will surely enter Paradise before them"? Or its meaning is: Indeed, We created them from a drop of semen just as We created all the children of Adam, and it is Our decree that no one enters Paradise except by faith, so why would one who has no faith be greedy to enter it?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 40:

﴿So I swear not by the Lord of the easts and the wests,﴾ — the risings of the sun and its settings —

﴿indeed We are able﴾

"Upon Our being able to replace them with better than them" (﴿عَلى أنْ نُبَدِّلَ خَيْرًا مِنهُمْ﴾), that is, upon Our destroying them and bringing about a creation more excellent than them and more obedient to Allah.

"And We are not to be outstripped" (﴿وَما نَحْنُ بِمَسْبُوقِينَ﴾), that is, not incapable of it.

{So leave them} — i.e., leave the deniers (al-mukadhdhibin),

{to plunge into their falsehood} — in their vain talk,

{and to play} — in their worldly life,

{until they meet their day which they are promised} — wherein is the punishment.

﴿يَوْمَ﴾ is a substitution (*badal*, a grammatical apposition) for "*yawmihim*."

﴿يَخْرُجُونَ﴾ is read with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and a *ḍamma* on the *rā'*, except by al-A'shā.

﴿مِنَ الأجْداثِ﴾ means "from the graves."

﴿سِراعًا﴾ is the plural of *sarī'* ("swift"), and it is a *ḥāl* (a circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject). It means "toward the caller."

﴿كَأنَّهُمْ﴾ is also a *ḥāl*.

﴿إلى نُصُبٍ﴾: Shāmī, Ḥafṣ and Sahl read *"nuṣbin"*; al-Mufaḍḍal reads *"naṣbin"*; and the others read it differently. A *nuṣub* is anything that is set up and worshipped besides God.

﴿يُوفِضُونَ﴾ means "they hasten."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 70, verse 44:

﴿Khashi'atan﴾ (humbled), a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in "yakhrujūn" (they come forth), meaning: abased,

﴿abṣāruhum﴾ (their eyes), meaning: they do not raise them, because of their abasement,

﴿tarhaquhum dhillatun﴾ (abasement covers them), meaning: humiliation overwhelms them,

﴿dhālika al-yawmu alladhī kānū yūʿadūn﴾ (That is the Day they were promised), in the world, and they used to deny it.
